body_markdown:
You found your Jordan hire. Now you're staring down SSC registration deadlines, Arabic language contract requirements, and a payroll system that only runs in Jordanian Dinar. None of that has to sit on your plate. This guide breaks down how an employer of record in Jordan handles the compliance side, what it costs compared to setting up your own entity, and how to figure out which path fits your situation.


**TLDR:**


- Jordan's Labour Law generally requires Social Security Corporation (SSC) registration from the date the employee joins work, per Jordan's Social Security Law, and ~14.25% employer contributions.
- Jordan's Labour Law generally requires wages to be paid by bank transfer in Jordanian Dinar, as cash payments are typically not permitted.
- Setting up a local entity takes 2 to 4 months, versus days through an EOR arrangement.
- Below higher headcounts, an EOR runs at 70% less cost than maintaining your own local entity.
- Bolto onboards new hires in Jordan in as little as 48 hours, including contract and SSC setup.


## What Is an Employer of Record in Jordan


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer of your team in Jordan on paper, while you keep directing their day-to-day work. Instead of setting up a Jordanian entity before you can hire compliantly, you partner with an EOR that already has the local registrations, employment contracts, and payroll setup in place. Bolto takes on that legal employer role for your Jordan-based hires, handling Arabic-language contract drafting, SSC registration, and payroll in Jordanian Dinar on your behalf. This model generally fits companies that want to hire in Jordan quickly, without months of entity setup, or whose headcount in the country isn't yet large enough to support running a local entity. You retain control over the role, the work, and the relationship with your hire, while Bolto absorbs the compliance and administrative obligations that come with Jordan's Labour Law.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Jordan


Hiring in Jordan means taking on a set of statutory obligations under Jordan's Labour Law, whether you handle them directly or through an[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) . Probation generally allows either side to end the arrangement without notice or compensation, but once an employee moves onto an indefinite contract, that flexibility typically narrows to a required one-month notice period, according to[Dentons' Jordan employment law guide](https://www.dentons.com/en/global-solutions/rules-regulations-and-laws-trackers/employment-and-labor-country-guides/jordan) .


The table below summarizes the core requirements you need to plan around.


Requirement General Rule


Probation period No notice or compensation typically required to end


Notice period (indefinite contracts) About 1 month or pay in lieu


Work week Sunday to Thursday


Employer SSC contribution Approximately 14.25% of salary (Jordan SSC, 2026)


SSC registration deadline Required from the date the employee joins work (Jordan Social Security Law)


Wage payment method Bank transfer in Jordanian Dinar, cash generally not accepted


Under Jordan's Labour Law, wages are generally required to be paid by bank transfer in Jordanian Dinar. Social Security Corporation (SSC) registration follows a fixed deadline under Jordan's Labour Law, and employer contributions add a cost to plan for from day one.


These figures reflect general rules under Jordan's labor code, and specifics can vary by sector, contract terms, and individual case. This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by situation and change over time, so consult a qualified employment lawyer for your specific circumstances.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Jordan: Which Is Right for You


There is no universal right answer here. An EOR and a local entity both get you to a compliant hire in Jordan, but they get you there on very different timelines, with different costs, and different amounts of control handed back to you. The best fit depends on how many people you are hiring, how fast you need them working, and how much say you want over benefits and equity down the line.


An EOR gets you compliant fast: your hire signs a contract, gets registered with the SSC, and starts receiving payroll in Jordanian Dinar within days, without you touching incorporation paperwork. A local entity gives you full legal and HR control, more flexibility on benefits and equity structuring, and a lower cost per employee once you are running a sizable team, but it takes roughly 2 to 4 months to set up and carries ongoing legal, accounting, and compliance overhead regardless of headcount. If you are hiring one or a handful of people in Jordan, or you are not yet sure how long the role will last, an EOR keeps your commitment light and your exit simple. Once your Jordanian headcount grows large enough to support dedicated local infrastructure, standing up your own entity generally becomes the more cost-effective path.
